claim: mCherry-JPH3 and mCherry-JPH4 induce the formation of ER-PM junctions in tsA201 cells.
source: Thin section electron microscopy confirmed the presence of ER-PM junctions in cells transfected with mCherry-JPH3 or mCherry-JPH4 (Figure 1B, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images showing ER-PM junctions in transfected cells (Figure 1B).

claim: ER-PM junctions in non-transfected tsA201 cells are infrequent (≥ 2 junctions in 8 % of cells, with a maximum of three junctions).
source: However, our previous analysis of thin sections demonstrated that ER-PM junctions in non-transfected tsA201 cells are infrequent (≥ 2 junctions in 8 % of cells, with a maximum of three junctions) and of small size (mean length of ~ 0.15 µm, maximum of 0.28 µm) (Perni et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Perni et al., 2017).

claim: ER-PM junctions in non-transfected tsA201 cells are of small size (mean length of ~ 0.15 µm, maximum of 0.28 µm).
source: However, our previous analysis of thin sections demonstrated that ER-PM junctions in non-transfected tsA201 cells are infrequent (≥ 2 junctions in 8 % of cells, with a maximum of three junctions) and of small size (mean length of ~ 0.15 µm, maximum of 0.28 µm) (Perni et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Perni et al., 2017).

claim: Two or more junctions were present in ~ 20 % of the cells transfected with a neuronal junctophilin.
source: By way of comparison, two or more junctions were present in ~ 20 % of the cells transfected with a neuronal junctophilin (about the same as the transfection efficiency).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of thin sections from transfected cells.

claim: Junctions induced by JPH3 or JPH4 are substantially longer than those in non-transfected cells.
source: These junctions were also substantially longer than those in non-transfected cells (the ones shown in Figure 1B, bottom panels, are roughly 0.55 and 0.77 µm for JPH3 and JPH4, respectively).
evidence: Supported by measurements from electron microscopy images (Figure 1B).

claim: The junctions induced by JPH3 or JPH4 have a relatively uniform gap of about ~ 7 nm separating the ER and PM.
source: Additionally, the junctions induced by JPH3 or JPH4 had a relatively uniform gap of about ~ 7 nm separating the ER and PM, which is similar to the gap in ER-PM junctions of dyspedic (RyR1-null) myotubes (Takekura et al., 1995), which endogenously express JPH2 (Felder et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by measurements from electron microscopy and comparison to published data (Takekura et al., 1995; Felder et al., 2002).

claim: JPH3 and JPH4 cause junctional accumulation of CaV1.2.
source: Co-expressed with either JPH3 (Figure 2B) or JPH4 (Figure 2C), the three high-voltage-activated (HVA) channels became concentrated in discrete regions that colocalized at the cell periphery with the junctophilins, whereas CaV3.1 did not.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing colocalization (Figure 2B, C) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 2D).

claim: JPH3 and JPH4 cause junctional accumulation of CaV2.1.
source: Co-expressed with either JPH3 (Figure 2B) or JPH4 (Figure 2C), the three high-voltage-activated (HVA) channels became concentrated in discrete regions that colocalized at the cell periphery with the junctophilins, whereas CaV3.1 did not.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing colocalization (Figure 2B, C) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 2E).

claim: JPH3 and JPH4 cause junctional accumulation of CaV2.2.
source: Co-expressed with either JPH3 (Figure 2B) or JPH4 (Figure 2C), the three high-voltage-activated (HVA) channels became concentrated in discrete regions that colocalized at the cell periphery with the junctophilins, whereas CaV3.1 did not.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing colocalization (Figure 2B, C) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 2F).

claim: JPH3 and JPH4 do not cause junctional accumulation of CaV3.1.
source: Co-expressed with either JPH3 (Figure 2B) or JPH4 (Figure 2C), the three high-voltage-activated (HVA) channels became concentrated in discrete regions that colocalized at the cell periphery with the junctophilins, whereas CaV3.1 did not.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images showing lack of colocalization (Figure 2B, C) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 2G).

claim: The mean colocalization coefficients for HVA channels with JPH3 or JPH4 ranged from 0.8 (CaV2.2/JPH4) down to 0.50 (CaV2.1/JPH3).
source: For the HVA channels, the mean colocalization coefficients ranged from 0.8 (CaV2.2/JPH4) down to 0.50 (CaV2.1/JPH3).
evidence: Supported by Pearson's coefficients calculated from confocal images (Figure 2D-F).

claim: The means for CaV3.1 colocalization with JPH3 (0.25) and JPH4 (0.35) were significantly (p < 0.0001) smaller than those for the HVA channels.
source: The means for CaV3.1 (0.25 vs. JPH3 and 0.35 versus JPH4) were significantly (p < 0.0001) smaller than those for the HVA channels (CaV1.2, CaV2.1, and CaV2.1) versus either JPH3 or JPH4.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of Pearson's coefficients (Figure 2G).

claim: The neuronal junctophilins recruit the P/Q channel CaV2.1 to ER-PM junctions in preference to the T-type channel CaV3.1.
source: One implication of these results is that the neuronal junctophilins recruit the P/Q channel CaV2.1 to ER-PM junctions in preference to the T-type channel CaV3.1, which is in good agreement with earlier results demonstrating that the AHP in Purkinje cells is preferentially triggered by P/Q channels (Womack et al., 2004) and that this AHP is greatly reduced when the two neuronal junctophilins are knocked out (Kakizawa et al., 2007).
evidence: Inference based on colocalization data and comparison to published electrophysiological results (Womack et al., 2004; Kakizawa et al., 2007).

claim: Neither JPH3 nor JPH4 caused large shifts in the peak I–V relationships for CaV1.2, CaV2.1, and CaV2.2.
source: Neither JPH3 nor JPH4 caused large shifts in the peak I–V relationships for any of these three channels (Figure 3A–C, top panels), indicating that the voltage dependence of activation was little affected.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements (Figure 3A-C, top panels).

claim: Macroscopic current densities were essentially unchanged for CaV1.2 and CaV2.2 but were slightly reduced for CaV2.1 when co-expressed with JPH3 or JPH4.
source: Macroscopic current densities were essentially unchanged for CaV1.2 and CaV2.2 but were slightly reduced for CaV2.1.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements (Figure 3).

claim: The neuronal junctophilins had little effect on the inactivation of calcium currents via the L-type channel CaV1.2.
source: The neuronal junctophilins had little effect on the inactivation of calcium currents via the L-type channel CaV1.2 (Figure 3A, lower panel) but slowed the inactivation of calcium currents via the non-L-type channels, CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 (Figure 3B, C, lower panels), with JPH4 having a greater effect than JPH3.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements (Figure 3A, lower panel).

claim: JPH3 and JPH4 slowed the inactivation of calcium currents via CaV2.1 and CaV2.2, with JPH4 having a greater effect than JPH3.
source: The neuronal junctophilins had little effect on the inactivation of calcium currents via the L-type channel CaV1.2 (Figure 3A, lower panel) but slowed the inactivation of calcium currents via the non-L-type channels, CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 (Figure 3B, C, lower panels), with JPH4 having a greater effect than JPH3.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements (Figure 3B, C, lower panels).

claim: JPH4 greatly slowed the inactivation of barium currents via CaV2.1 and CaV2.2.
source: As for calcium currents, the inactivation of barium currents via CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 was greatly slowed by JPH4, which had less effect on barium currents via CaV1.2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: JPH4 had less effect on barium currents via CaV1.2 compared to CaV2.1 and CaV2.2.
source: As for calcium currents, the inactivation of barium currents via CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 was greatly slowed by JPH4, which had less effect on barium currents via CaV1.2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: JPH3(1 – 707) and JPH4(1 – 576) lack the small segment of the C-terminus that traverses the ER membrane and thus retain the ability to associate with the surface membrane but not to induce ER-PM junctions.
source: To ascertain whether the slowing of inactivation required the formation of ER-PM junctions, we also tested the effects of JPH3(1 – 707) and JPH4(1 – 576), which lack the small segment of the C-terminus that traverses the ER membrane (Figure 1A) and thus retain the ability to associate with the surface membrane (leftmost panels of Figure 10A, B) but not to induce ER-PM junctions.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images (Figure 10A, B) and structural information (Figure 1A).

claim: JPH3(1 – 707) and JPH4(1 – 576) slowed inactivation of CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 to an extent that was similar to, or greater than, that of the full-length constructs.
source: Nonetheless, JPH3(1 – 707) and JPH4(1 – 576) slowed inactivation of CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 (Figure 4A, B) to an extent that was similar to, or greater than, that of the full-length constructs (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements (Figure 4A, B) compared to Figure 3.

claim: The slowing of inactivation is consistent with a direct interaction between the channels and junctophilins.
source: These results are consistent with the possibility that the slowing of inactivation is a consequence of a direct interaction between the channels and junctophilins, and that truncated JPH3 interacts with a larger fraction of CaV2.1 channels in the membrane than does full-length JPH3.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that truncated junctophilins lacking ER-spanning segments still slow inactivation.

claim: Truncated JPH3 interacts with a larger fraction of CaV2.1 channels in the membrane than does full-length JPH3.
source: These results are consistent with the possibility that the slowing of inactivation is a consequence of a direct interaction between the channels and junctophilins, and that truncated JPH3 interacts with a larger fraction of CaV2.1 channels in the membrane than does full-length JPH3.
evidence: Inference based on the greater slowing of inactivation by truncated JPH3 compared to full-length JPH3.

claim: For JPH3, the highest colocalization occurred with RyR1, with slightly less colocalization with RyR3, and significantly less with RyR2.
source: The corresponding Pearson's coefficients (Figure 5C) reveal that for JPH3 the highest colocation occurred with RyR1, with slightly less colocalization with RyR3, and significantly less with RyR2.
evidence: Supported by Pearson's coefficients calculated from confocal images (Figure 5C).

claim: For JPH4, the greatest colocalization occurred with RyR3, whereas there was significantly less colocalization with both RyR1 and RyR2.
source: For JPH4, the greatest colocalization occurred with RyR3, whereas there was significantly less colocalization with both RyR1 and RyR2.
evidence: Supported by Pearson's coefficients calculated from confocal images (Figure 5C).

claim: The colocalization of RyR3 with JPH4 was not significantly (p = 0.98) different from the colocalization of RyR2 with JPH3.
source: The colocalization of RyR3 with JPH4 was not significantly (p = 0.98) different from the colocalization of RyR2 with JPH3.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of Pearson's coefficients (Figure 5C).

claim: For any given RyR isoform, the colocalization with JPH4 was significantly (p < 0.0001) lower than with JPH3.
source: However, for any given RyR isoform, the colocalization with JPH4 was significantly (p < 0.0001) lower than with JPH3.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of Pearson's coefficients (Figure 5C).

claim: The greater effectiveness of JPH3 in causing the accumulation of RyRs may help to explain why single knockout of JPH3 affects neurological function, whereas single knockout of JPH4 does not.
source: Based on these results, it seems that the greater effectiveness of JPH3 in causing the accumulation of RyRs may help to explain why single knockout of JPH3 affects neurological function, whereas single knockout of JPH4 does not.
evidence: Inference based on differential RyR recruitment by JPH3 and JPH4, and comparison to published knockout phenotypes.

claim: The levels of endogenously expressed RyRs in tsA201 cells were negligible compared to those of the heterologously expressed RyRs.
source: Thus, it appears that the levels of endogenously expressed RyRs were negligible compared to those of the heterologously expressed RyRs.
evidence: Supported by caffeine-induced calcium transient measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: The additional presence of CaV1.2 did not have a significant effect either on the colocalization of RyR2 with JPH3 or on the colocalization of RyR3 with JPH4.
source: The additional presence of CaV1.2 did not have a significant effect either on the colocalization of RyR2 with JPH3 or on the colocalization of RyR3 with JPH4.
evidence: Supported by Pearson's coefficients (Figure 6).

claim: JPH3 caused CaV2.1 to colocalize with RyR1.
source: These indicate that JPH3 caused CaV2.1 to colocalize with RyR1, consistent with its ability to recruit not only CaV2.1 (Figure 2), but also RyR1 (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by Pearson's coefficients (Figure 7B) and confocal images (Figure 7A).

claim: JPH4 failed to cause colocalization of CaV2.1 with RyR1.
source: Contrastingly, JPH4, which recruited CaV2.1 (Figure 2) but not RyR1 (Figure 5), failed to cause colocalization of CaV2.1 with RyR1 (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: Supported by Pearson's coefficients (Figure 7B) and confocal images (Figure 7A).

claim: JPH3, but not JPH4, caused CaV2.2 to colocalize with RyR1.
source: A similar pattern was observed for CaV2.2: JPH3, but not JPH4, caused CaV2.2 to colocalize with RyR1 (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: Supported by Pearson's coefficients (Figure 7D) and confocal images (Figure 7C).

claim: ER calcium release can occur in cells expressing JPH3, RyR1, and either CaV2.1 or CaV2.2.
source: Furthermore, it appeared that ER calcium release could occur in cells expressing JPH3, RyR1, and either CaV2.1 or CaV2.2 (Figure 7E–J).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments showing Fluo8 and R-CEPIAer transients (Figure 7E-J).

claim: About a third of cells stably transfected with RyR1 and transiently transfected with CaV2.1 or CaV2.2, R-CEPIA-er and CFP-JPH3 that produced cytoplasmic calcium transients in response to KCl depolarization also showed a concomitant release of calcium from the ER.
source: More specifically, of the cells stably transfected with RyR1, and transiently transfected with CaV2.1 or CaV2.2, R-CEPIA-er and CFP-JPH3, about a third that produced cytoplasmic calcium transients in response to KCl depolarization, also showed a concomitant release of calcium from the ER.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments (Figure 7E-J).

claim: The data are consistent with, but do not prove, that both CaV2.1 or CaV2.2 can trigger activation of RyR1 at junctions induced by JPH3.
source: Given these limitations, the strongest statement that can be made is that the data in Figure 7D–J are consistent with, but do not prove, that both CaV2.1 or CaV2.2 can trigger activation of RyR1 at junctions induced by JPH3.
evidence: Inference based on calcium imaging data (Figure 7D-J) with acknowledged limitations.

claim: Colocalization of RyR1 with JPH3 appeared to depend on the JPH3 divergent domain.
source: Because colocalization of RyR1 with JPH3 appeared to depend on the JPH3 divergent domain (Figure 8), we tested for interactions between RyR11:4300 and constructs containing varying sized fragments of this divergent domain.
evidence: Supported by colocalization data with JPH3-with-JPH4-divergent chimera (Figure 8).

claim: The JPH3-with-JPH4-divergent chimera failed to cause accumulation of either RyR1 or RyR2, and had a reduced ability to recruit RyR3.
source: However, unlike JPH3, the chimera failed to cause accumulation of either RyR1 or RyR2, and had a reduced ability to recruit RyR3 (Figure 8B, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by confocal images (Figure 8B) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 8C).

claim: The presence of the JPH4 divergent domain was sufficient to cause the chimera to behave more like JPH4 than JPH3 with respect to RyR recruitment.
source: Thus, the presence of the JPH4 divergent domain was sufficient to cause the chimera to behave more like JPH4 than JPH3, a pattern that was also evident in Figure 8C, which compares Pearson's coefficients for colocalization of the three RyR isoforms with JPH3 (left), the chimera (center), and JPH4 (right).
evidence: Supported by Pearson's coefficients (Figure 8C).

claim: The JPH3-with-JPH4-divergent chimera was effective at recruiting CaV1.2 to junctions.
source: Specifically, a comparison of Pearson's coefficients (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) indicates that the JPH3-with-JPH4-divergent chimera was effective at recruiting CaV1.2 to junctions.
evidence: Supported by Pearson's coefficients (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The JPH3-with-JPH4-divergent chimera slowed the inactivation of both CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 to an extent that was similar to that of JPH3 and not to the larger slowing caused by JPH4.
source: Moreover, this chimera slowed the inactivation of both CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) to an extent that was similar to that of JPH3 and not to the larger slowing caused by JPH4.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).

claim: RyR11:4300 and RyR31:4032 accumulated at JPH3-induced junctions.
source: In particular, the fluorescence associated with YFP-RyR11:4300 and YFP-RyR31:4032 accumulated at JPH3-induced junctions, which caused their fluorescence to be increased relative to regions lacking junctions (Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by confocal images (Figure 9A) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 9D, F).

claim: The accumulation of YFP-RyR11:4300 and YFP-RyR31:4032 at JPH3-induced junctions implies that these constructs bound to a component(s) present in these junctions, with JPH3 itself being an obvious candidate.
source: The accumulation of YFP-RyR11:4300 and YFP-RyR31:4032 at JPH3-induced junctions implies that these constructs bound to a component(s) present in these junctions, with JPH3 itself being an obvious candidate.
evidence: Inference based on the observed accumulation of RyR cytoplasmic domains at junctions.

claim: If it is assumed that the binding of YFP-RyR11:4300 and YFP-RyR31:4032 indicates that they took on near-native conformations, it would imply that the cytoplasmic domains of the full-length RyR1 and RyR3 bind to JPH3 and thus help retain these RyRs at ER-PM junctions.
source: If it is assumed that the binding of YFP-RyR11:4300 and YFP-RyR31:4032 indicates that they took on near-native conformations, it would imply that the cytoplasmic domains of the full-length RyR1 and RyR3 bind to JPH3 and thus help retain these RyRs at ER-PM junctions.
evidence: Inference based on the behavior of RyR cytoplasmic domain constructs.

claim: RyR11:4300 colocalized with JPH3(1 – 707).
source: Much like JPH3(1 – 707) itself, JPH4(1 – 576)-JPH3(418 – 707) appeared to reduce the mobility of YFP-RyR11:4300 at the cell surface, as might be expected if the RyR1 cytoplasmic domain and JPH3 divergent domain interacted with one another.
evidence: Supported by photobleaching experiments (Figure 10A) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 10F).

claim: JPH4(1 – 576)-JPH3(418 – 707) appeared to reduce the mobility of YFP-RyR11:4300 at the cell surface.
source: Much like JPH3(1 – 707) itself, JPH4(1 – 576)-JPH3(418 – 707) appeared to reduce the mobility of YFP-RyR11:4300 at the cell surface, as might be expected if the RyR1 cytoplasmic domain and JPH3 divergent domain interacted with one another.
evidence: Supported by photobleaching experiments (Figure 10B) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 10F).

claim: RyR11:4300 colocalized with mCherry-JPH3(418 – 748).
source: Cells transfected with YFP-RyR11:4300 together with either mCherry-JPH3(418 – 748) or JPH3(653 – 748)-mCherry are illustrated in Figure 10C, D. These junctophilin constructs had the reticular distribution expected for an ER localization, and YFP-RyR11:4300 colocalized both with mCherry-JPH3(418 – 748) and with JPH3(653 – 748)-mCherry.
evidence: Supported by confocal images (Figure 10C) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 10F).

claim: RyR11:4300 colocalized with JPH3(653 – 748)-mCherry.
source: Cells transfected with YFP-RyR11:4300 together with either mCherry-JPH3(418 – 748) or JPH3(653 – 748)-mCherry are illustrated in Figure 10C, D. These junctophilin constructs had the reticular distribution expected for an ER localization, and YFP-RyR11:4300 colocalized both with mCherry-JPH3(418 – 748) and with JPH3(653 – 748)-mCherry.
evidence: Supported by confocal images (Figure 10D) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 10F).

claim: Little colocalization occurred between YFP-RyR11:4300 and mCherry-ER.
source: As an alternative, cells transfected with YFP-RyR11:4300 and mCherry-ER were used as a control. Little colocalization occurred between YFP-RyR11:4300 and mCherry-ER (Figure 10E).
evidence: Supported by confocal images (Figure 10E) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 10F).

claim: The colocalization of YFP-RyR11:4300 differed little between JPH3(418 – 748), which contained the entire divergent region, and JPH3(653 – 748), which contained only the final approximately fourth of the divergent region.
source: Pearson's coefficients for the various construct combinations (Figure 10F) indicate that the colocalization of YFP-RyR11:4300 differed little between JPH3(418 – 748), which contained the entire divergent region, and JPH3(653 – 748), which contained only the final approximately fourth of the divergent region.
evidence: Supported by Pearson's coefficients (Figure 10F).

claim: The site of interaction with the RyR1 cytoplasmic domain is contained within JPH3 residues 653 – 707.
source: These results, taken together with the colocalization of YFP-RyR11:4300 with JPH4(1 – 576)-JPH3(418 – 707), as shown in Figure 10B, indicate that the site of interaction with the RyR1 cytoplasmic domain is contained within JPH3 residues 653 – 707.
evidence: Inference based on colocalization data with various JPH3 constructs (Figure 10).

claim: Deletion of JPH3 divergent domain residues 681 – 725 does not affect junctional recruitment of full-length RyR1.
source: Lastly, the observation that deletion of JPH3 divergent domain residues 681 – 725 does not affect junctional recruitment of full-length RyR1 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1) suggests a further shortening of the candidate region to JPH3 residues 653 – 680.
evidence: Supported by colocalization data with JPH3Δ681-725 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).

claim: JPH3 residues 653 – 680 contain the site that appears to be important for binding to the cytoplasmic domain of RyR1.
source: Thus, we propose that JPH3 residues 653 – 680 contain the site that appears to be important for binding to the cytoplasmic domain of RyR1.
evidence: Inference based on colocalization data with various JPH3 constructs (Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).

claim: JPH3 residues 653 – 680 are strongly conserved across a number of vertebrate species.
source: This 28-residue segment is strongly conserved across a number of vertebrate species (Figure 12).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment (Figure 12).

claim: YFP-RyR31:4032 did not colocalize with mCherry-JPH3(1 – 707).
source: Although there was a prominent band of red fluorescence at the cell surface, the images acquired before photobleaching show that the concentration of YFP-RyR31:4032 was nearly uniform throughout the cell, and images after photobleaching indicate that all of the YFP-RyR31:4032 was relatively mobile.
evidence: Supported by photobleaching experiments (Figure 11A) and Pearson's coefficients (Figure 11B).

claim: The cytoplasmic YFP fluorescence intensity was 92.7 ± 22.1 (n = 14, range 22.4– 282.3) for YFP-RyR31:4032 and 1497.9 ± 317.8 (n = 16, range 80.4– 4783.4) for YFP-RyR11:4300.
source: Specifically, an analysis that takes into account that the confocal acquisition parameters varied from cell to cell (see Materials and methods) indicates that the cytoplasmic YFP fluorescence intensity (mean ± SEM in arbitrary units) was 92.7 ± 22.1 (n = 14, range 22.4– 282.3) for YFP-RyR31:4032 and 1497.9 ± 317.8 (n = 16, range 80.4– 4783.4) for YFP-RyR11:4300.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity measurements.

claim: CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 may participate in interactions with JPH3 and JPH4, which are similar to those occurring between the CaV1 channels and muscle junctophilins.
source: Thus, it may be that CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 participate in interactions with JPH3 and JPH4, which are similar to those occurring between the CaV1 channels and muscle junctophilins.
evidence: Speculation based on sequence conservation of junctophilin-binding motifs.

claim: The search for potential sites of interaction between CaV2.1 or CaV2.2 and the neuronal junctophilins will have to proceed de novo because neither of the CaV2 C-termini contain a junctophilin-interacting motif like that in the CaV1 C-termini.
source: The search for potential sites of interaction between CaV2.1 or CaV2.2 and the neuronal junctophilins will have to proceed de novo because neither of the CaV2 C-termini contain a junctophilin-interacting motif like that in the CaV1 C-termini.
evidence: Inference based on sequence analysis.

claim: For the CaV2 channels, it will be important to determine whether a single site of interaction accounts for both selective retention at junctions and the slowing of inactivation.
source: For the CaV2 channels, it will also be important to determine whether a single site of interaction accounts for both selective retention at junctions and the slowing of inactivation.
evidence: Speculation about future research directions.

claim: In brain regions expressing all three RyR isoforms, RyR1 and RyR3 may be preferentially recruited to junctions containing JPH3.
source: Thus, in brain regions expressing all three RyR isoforms, RyR1 and RyR3 may be preferentially recruited to junctions containing JPH3.
evidence: Inference based on colocalization data (Figure 5).

claim: This differential recruitment of RyRs may at least partially account for why there was no apparent behavioral phenotype observed for knockout of JPH4 only, a detectable phenotype (motor discoordination) for knockout of JPH3 only, and a broad range of neurological deficits for knockout of both JPH3 and JPH4.
source: This differential recruitment of RyRs may at least partially account for why there was no apparent behavioral phenotype observed for knockout of JPH4 only (Moriguchi et al., 2006), a detectable phenotype (motor discoordination) for knockout of JPH3 only (Nishi et al., 2002), and a broad range of neurological deficits for knockout of both JPH3 and JPH4 (Moriguchi et al., 2006).
evidence: Inference based on differential RyR recruitment and comparison to published knockout phenotypes (Moriguchi et al., 2006; Nishi et al., 2002).

claim: The lower colocalization of RyR2 with JPH3 and RyR3 with JPH4 could be a consequence of the presence of RyRs in both junctional and non-junctional ER.
source: However, the lower colocalization cannot be taken as indicating a lesser functional importance in neuronal calcium signaling. The lower colocalization could be a consequence of the presence of RyRs in both junctional and non-junctional ER.
evidence: Speculation about the interpretation of colocalization data.

claim: RyRs at the junctions would be required for the initial calcium release triggered by calcium entering across the plasma membrane, whereas those in non-junctional ER could increase the spatial spread of the cytoplasmic calcium transient.
source: Those at the junctions would be required for the initial calcium release triggered by calcium entering across the plasma membrane, whereas those in non-junctional ER could increase the spatial spread of the cytoplasmic calcium transient.
evidence: Speculation about the functional roles of junctional and non-junctional RyRs.

claim: Precedent for RyRs in both junctional and non-junctional ER is provided by contractile cells of the heart in which RyR2 is located not only in the junctional SR, where it is activated by calcium entry via CaV1.2, but also in non-junctional ('corbular') SR.
source: Precedent for this idea is provided by contractile cells of the heart in which RyR2 is located not only in the junctional SR, where it is activated by calcium entry via CaV1.2, but also in non-junctional ('corbular') SR (Dolber and Sommer, 1984; Jewett et al., 1971).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work on cardiac muscle (Dolber and Sommer, 1984; Jewett et al., 1971).

claim: JPH3 and JPH4 induce ER-PM junctions and display isoform specificity in controlling the molecular architecture of the junctions.
source: Our results suggest that JPH3 and JPH4 (1) induce ER-PM junctions and display isoform specificity in controlling the molecular architecture of the junctions and (2) serve not only to establish these calcium-signaling microdomains but also to functionally modulate at least some of the junctional proteins, as was directly demonstrated for CaV2.1 and CaV2.2.
evidence: Summary of findings from the study.

claim: JPH3 and JPH4 serve not only to establish calcium-signaling microdomains but also to functionally modulate at least some of the junctional proteins, as was directly demonstrated for CaV2.1 and CaV2.2.
source: Our results suggest that JPH3 and JPH4 (1) induce ER-PM junctions and display isoform specificity in controlling the molecular architecture of the junctions and (2) serve not only to establish these calcium-signaling microdomains but also to functionally modulate at least some of the junctional proteins, as was directly demonstrated for CaV2.1 and CaV2.2.
evidence: Summary of findings from the study.

claim: In skeletal muscle, ER-PM junctions (triads) are the site at which functional coupling occurs between CaV1.1 in the plasma membrane and RyR1 in the ER.
